title: Chana Masala Recipe: Restaurant-Style Chole at Home in 30 Minutes
excerpt: A simple 30-minute chana masala (chole) recipe with the right spice balance, plus tips to get restaurant-style depth at home.
contentHtml:
Few dishes are as comforting as a bowl of hot chole with bhature or steamed rice. The good news: you don't need a long ingredient list to get that deep, tangy, restaurant-style flavour. You need good chickpeas, patient onions and a well-balanced masala.

Ingredients (serves 4)

  • 1½ cups chickpeas (kabuli chana), soaked overnight
  • 2 medium onions, finely chopped
  • 2 tomatoes, pureed
  • 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
  • 2 tbsp oil or ghee
  • 1 tbsp Ruchi Chhole Masala
  • ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp red chilli powder, salt to taste
  • 1 tsp kasuri methi and fresh coriander to finish

Method

  1. Cook the chickpeas. Pressure-cook the soaked chickpeas with salt for 4 to 5 whistles until soft but not mushy. Keep the cooking water.
  2. Brown the onions. Heat oil, add the onions and cook on medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until deep golden. This step builds most of the flavour, so don't rush it.
  3. Add the base. Stir in ginger-garlic paste for a minute, then add the tomato puree, turmeric and chilli powder. Cook until the oil separates.
  4. Add the masala. Add the chhole masala and cook for 30 seconds so the spices bloom.
  5. Simmer. Add the chickpeas and about 1 cup of the cooking water. Simmer for 10 to 12 minutes, lightly mashing a few chickpeas to thicken the gravy.
  6. Finish. Crush the kasuri methi between your palms, sprinkle it over, and garnish with coriander.

Tips for better chole

  • Cooking the chickpeas with a tea bag or a pinch of baking soda gives a darker colour, a common restaurant trick.
  • A squeeze of lemon or a pinch of amchur at the end lifts the tang.
  • Let the chole rest for 10 minutes; the flavours settle and the gravy thickens.

What to serve with it

Chole pairs well with bhature, kulcha, jeera rice or plain roti, along with sliced onions and a green chilli on the side.

title: Whole Spices vs Ground Spices: Which Should You Use and When?
excerpt: Whole or ground? Learn how each form behaves in cooking, how long it stays fresh, and which one to reach for in common Indian dishes.
contentHtml:
Walk into any Indian kitchen and you will find both whole spices in the tempering tin and ground spices in the masala box. They are not interchangeable. Each form releases flavour differently, so choosing the right one makes a visible difference to your food.

How whole spices behave

Whole spices such as cumin, mustard seeds, cloves, cardamom and cinnamon keep their essential oils locked inside until heat or crushing releases them. That is why they are used in tadka (tempering): hot oil draws the aroma out and carries it through the dish. Whole spices also stay fresh longer when stored properly.

  • Best for: tempering, rice dishes like biryani and pulao, slow-cooked gravies, pickling.
  • Examples: whole cumin, mustard seeds, panch phoran.

How ground spices behave

Ground spices have a larger surface area, so they dissolve into a dish and flavour it evenly and quickly. The trade-off is that they lose aroma faster once opened.

  • Best for: gravies, marinades, dry rubs, quick sabzis, dals.
  • Examples: turmeric powder, black pepper powder, garam masala.

Quick comparison

Whole Ground
Flavour release Slow, builds with heat Fast, blends evenly
Shelf life Longer Shorter once opened
Typical use Tadka, rice, pickles Gravies, marinades

Can you swap one for the other?

Sometimes. As a rough guide, use about half the quantity of a ground spice when replacing the whole one, and add it later in the cooking so it does not burn. Whole spices swapped in for ground ones will not blend into a smooth gravy, so grind them first.

Storage tips

  • Keep spices in airtight containers away from sunlight, heat and moisture.
  • Use a dry spoon every time.
  • Buy in quantities you will finish within a few months, especially ground spices.

title: 5 Everyday Indian Spices and How They Fit Into a Balanced Diet
excerpt: Turmeric, cumin, black pepper, mustard and fennel are staples of Indian cooking. Here is how to use them every day in simple, balanced meals.
contentHtml:
Spices do more than add flavour. They are the heart of everyday Indian cooking and make simple, home-cooked food more satisfying without relying on heavy sauces. Here are five staples worth keeping in reach, and easy ways to use them.

1. Turmeric (Haldi)

Turmeric gives dals and sabzis their warm golden colour and earthy taste. A pinch at the start of cooking is enough for most dishes. Try our turmeric powder in dal tadka or vegetable curries.

2. Cumin (Jeera)

Cumin is among the most used spices in India. Roast it for raita, temper it in ghee for dal, or add ground cumin to marinades. Stock both whole jeera and ground cumin.

3. Black Pepper (Kali Mirch)

Freshly ground black pepper adds gentle heat to soups, salads, eggs and masala chai. Our black pepper powder is a quick way to finish a dish.

4. Mustard Seeds (Sarson / Rai)

Popping mustard seeds in hot oil is the start of countless South and East Indian dishes, from curd rice to vegetable stir-fries. See our mustard seeds.

5. Fennel (Saunf)

Fennel is both a cooking spice and a traditional after-meal refresher. Chew a few seeds after dinner, or add them to tea and pickles.

Putting it into a daily plate

  • Build meals around dal, vegetables, whole grains and curd.
  • Use spices for flavour so you can go easier on added salt and oil.
  • Choose fresh, properly packed spices and store them airtight.

This article is for general information and is not medical advice. If you have a health condition or allergies, speak to a qualified professional about your diet.

title: How to Make Perfect Elaichi Chai: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: Brew a fragrant cup of cardamom tea with the right tea-to-milk ratio, timing and tips for a strong, aromatic chai.
contentHtml:
A good cup of elaichi chai is simple, but small details decide whether it tastes flat or fragrant. Here is a reliable method for two cups.

What you need

  • 2 cups water
  • 1 cup full-cream milk (adjust to taste)
  • 2 heaped tsp Ruchi Elaichi Chai (or tea leaves plus 2 crushed green cardamom pods)
  • Sugar or jaggery to taste

Steps

  1. Boil the water. Bring the water to a rolling boil in a saucepan.
  2. Add the tea. Add the elaichi tea and let it boil for 1 to 2 minutes until the water darkens and the aroma rises.
  3. Add the milk. Pour in the milk and bring it back to a boil.
  4. Simmer. Lower the heat and simmer for 2 to 3 minutes for a stronger, kadak cup. Add sugar to taste.
  5. Strain and serve. Pour through a strainer into cups and serve hot.

Tips for a better cup

  • Use fresh water each time; reboiled water tastes flat.
  • Crush the cardamom just before use if you add extra pods; the aroma fades quickly.
  • Don't over-boil after adding milk or the tea can turn bitter.
  • Adjust strength by changing simmer time rather than adding more tea.

Serving ideas

Elaichi chai goes well with rusk, biscuits, pakoras or a plate of bhaji. For a stronger everyday brew, try our Utkal Dust Chai.

title: Easy Pasta Recipes for Busy Weeknights (Ready in 20 Minutes)
excerpt: Three quick pasta ideas, from masala penne to creamy fusilli, plus tips to cook durum wheat pasta perfectly every time.
contentHtml:
When dinner needs to be quick, pasta is a dependable answer. Made from durum wheat semolina, it cooks in minutes and works with Indian-style flavours as well as classic sauces. Here are three simple ideas and the basics for cooking pasta well.

How to cook pasta perfectly

  1. Use a large pot: about 1 litre of water per 100 g of pasta.
  2. Salt the water once it boils.
  3. Add the pasta and stir in the first minute so it doesn't stick.
  4. Cook according to the pack time, tasting a minute early for a firm bite.
  5. Reserve a cup of pasta water, then drain. Don't rinse if you will add sauce.

1. Masala Penne

Saute onion, garlic and capsicum in oil, add tomato puree and a spoon of garam masala, then toss in cooked penne. Finish with a splash of pasta water and fresh coriander.

2. Creamy Fusilli with Vegetables

Make a light white sauce with butter, flour and milk, add sweet corn, broccoli and a pinch of black pepper, then fold in fusilli. The spirals hold the sauce well.

3. Garlic-Chilli Pasta

Warm olive oil with sliced garlic and chilli flakes, toss in cooked pasta and a handful of herbs. Ready in the time it takes to boil the water.

Pantry tips

  • Keep one short shape (penne, fusilli) and one tube shape on hand.
  • Store pasta in a cool, dry place in an airtight container.
  • Pair with the Ruchi noodles range when you want a different quick meal.
